title: The 'Hey Now' Episode

jokes.text: "Wow" backwards is "wow." Did you know that?
jokes.setup: Guest mentions they went to Egypt, Larry says "Wow"
jokes.punchline: "Wow" backwards is "wow" — a palindrome observation delivered as if it's a revelation
jokes.explanation: Clean wordplay with good economy — the palindrome observation is a reliable crowd-pleaser. Not particularly original but well-constructed as a quick verbal gag.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: "Wow" backwards is "wow." Did you know that?

jokes.text: "Wow" upside-down is "Mom," and Mom upside-down is Dad's favorite thing.
jokes.setup: "Wow" backwards is "wow" — building on the palindrome bit
jokes.punchline: Mom upside-down is "WOW" which is "Dad's favorite thing" — a sly sexual implication about the parents
jokes.explanation: The escalation from the palindrome joke to a sly sex-about-parents punchline is clever construction. Each step logically follows, and the payoff is risqué but earned. Good economy and structure for stand-up.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: "Wow" upside-down is "Mom," and Mom upside-down is Dad's favorite thing

jokes.text: We went to Egypt with my in-laws who are a lot of fun... if you like being in a vault with them.
jokes.setup: Describing in-laws as fun travel companions
jokes.punchline: "If you like being in a vault with them" — claustrophobic, suffocating, tomb imagery playing on the Egypt setting
jokes.explanation: The vault image cleverly doubles as tomb/Egypt reference and suffocating-in-laws metaphor. Economical and well-placed. The self-aware follow-up 'I don't know what that means' is the funnier beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We went to Egypt with my in-laws who are a lot of fun... if you like being in a vault with them

jokes.text: "I don't know what that means, but thank you for laughing."
jokes.setup: Audience laughs at the in-laws/vault joke
jokes.punchline: Comic admits he doesn't actually know what his own joke means — meta acknowledgment of the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Genuinely sharp self-aware comedy. Breaking the performer-audience contract by admitting the joke was hollow but gratefully accepting the laugh anyway. Very economical. Funnier than the original vault joke it follows.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I don't know what that means, but thank you for laughing

jokes.text: We went to the Sphinx. We went to the back of the Sphinx. But nobody ever goes there because it Sphinx back there.
jokes.setup: Setting up the tourist trip to the Sphinx
jokes.punchline: "It Sphinx back there" — homophonic pun on "stinks"
jokes.explanation: A groan-worthy pun that works purely on phonetic cleverness. Low originality — Sphinx/stinks is a well-worn joke territory — but it's cleanly executed. The setup is a bit labored for the payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: But nobody ever goes there because it Sphinx back there

jokes.text: It's interesting. All the women look like Jamie Farr.
jokes.setup: Describing Egyptian sightseeing
jokes.punchline: The absurd specificity of Jamie Farr as the comparison point for Egyptian women
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Jamie Farr' over a generic comparison is what makes it land — it's an unexpected and funny image. Slight ethnic stereotype underlying it, but the absurdist specificity elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: All the women look like Jamie Farr

jokes.text: I'm a big Jamie Farr fan and I love women, so the combination just turned me on major. Major... that's from MASH too.
jokes.setup: Jamie Farr turns me on — then catches himself on the word "major"
jokes.punchline: "Major... that's from MASH too" — self-interrupting callback to MASH after accidentally using military terminology
jokes.explanation: Smart mid-sentence self-interruption that mines MASH lingo organically. The callback is earned because the comic himself catches the unintentional MASH reference, making it feel spontaneous and clever rather than planted.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm a big Jamie Farr fan and I love women... so the combination just turned me on major

jokes.text: You're negotiating. There's a guy under your stall reaching in. You're exchanging the money, hoping you can just... 'Give the money.' 'Give me the paper.'
jokes.setup: Egyptian airport bathroom requires tipping for toilet paper
jokes.punchline: The tense transactional exchange with a stranger under a bathroom stall, framed as hostage-negotiation-style standoff
jokes.explanation: Good observational comedy grounded in a specific, universal anxiety — paying for bathroom paper in foreign countries. The negotiation framing elevates a mundane observation into a vivid, funny image.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Major... that's from MASH too

jokes.text: I gave him $17 for three sheets of toilet paper. I realized you're better off just using the currency — getting a wad of bills and hoping you don't get chaffed.
jokes.setup: Didn't understand the currency at the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Better to use the worthless currency bills as toilet paper — hoping you don't get chafed by the paper money
jokes.explanation: Sharp escalation — from overpaying for toilet paper to using currency AS toilet paper. The 'chaffed' detail is a funny, specific, physical concern that sells the absurdity. Well-structured payoff with good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: There's a guy under your stall reaching in

jokes.text: Hank, have you ever been in the Middle East? Indeed I am.
jokes.setup: Comic asks Hank if he's ever been to the Middle East
jokes.punchline: Hank responds "Indeed I am" — present tense, as if he IS currently in the Middle East, grammatically confused or self-importantly vague
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Hank. His pompous "Indeed I am" in present tense when asked if he's EVER been somewhere is a wonderful character beat — self-important, grammatically confused, delivered with total confidence. Pure Hank Kingsley character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I realized you're better off just using the currency... getting a wad of bills and hoping you don't get chaffed

jokes.text: I believe Hank was just then in the Middle East.
jokes.setup: Hank's bizarre "Indeed I am" response
jokes.punchline: The comic deadpans to the audience that Hank was apparently mentally transported there just now
jokes.explanation: The deadpan callback to Hank's non-sequitur is efficiently done. The comic treats Hank's confused grammar as an event that literally happened, which is a clean and funny way to play it.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Indeed I am

jokes.text: He said, 'I have a problem. The Earth just came out of me.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Marvin came out of the restroom at the Egyptian airport looking distressed after bad food
jokes.punchline: "The Earth just came out of me" — euphemism for catastrophic digestive event on a biblical scale
jokes.explanation: This is legitimately excellent stand-up writing. 'The Earth just came out of me' is an extraordinarily economical, original, and quotable euphemism for a traveler's stomach event. The scale of 'Earth' for what would normally be a much coarser statement is inspired. Highly quotable and nearly unprecedented phrasing. One of the episode's peaks.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I believe Hank was just then in the Middle East

jokes.text: When you get close to him, but then when he's Farr, forget it.
jokes.setup: Dr. Marvin also looks like Jamie Farr
jokes.punchline: "When he's Farr, forget it" — homophonic pun on 'far' and Jamie Farr's last name
jokes.explanation: Another Jamie Farr name-pun, competently constructed but trading on the same territory as the earlier joke. The callback earns it some credit but it's a weaker pun than the surrounding material.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Marvin
dialogue.line: The Earth just came out of me

jokes.text: I didn't even need to be there for the fuckin' Saget interview. All I said was 'Hi, Bob. Bye, Bob.' I could've been working at a Jack In The Box.
jokes.setup: Post-show backstage, Larry is clearly stewing about being underutilized in the Bob Saget interview
jokes.punchline: "I could've been working at a Jack In The Box" — reducing the prestigious late-night host gig to irrelevance with a fast-food comparison
jokes.explanation: Pure Larry Sanders character comedy — the paranoid, insecure host reducing his entire professional purpose to irrelevance. 'Jack In The Box' is perfectly chosen; specific, deflating, funny. The self-pity framed as rage is quintessentially Larry. High character integration.

dialogue.line: When you get close to him, but then when he's Farr, forget it

jokes.text: Don't diminish yourself. Anyone with less talent would've tried to interrupt.
jokes.setup: Larry complains he barely participated in the Saget interview
jokes.punchline: Artie's backhanded compliment reframes Larry's passivity as a talent — the talent of knowing when to shut up
jokes.explanation: Exceptional writing. Artie's line is simultaneously a genuine compliment, a devastating put-down, and a perfect character moment — the veteran producer managing his volatile star. 'Anyone with less talent would've tried to interrupt' inverts the expected compliment structure brilliantly. This is what Rip Torn's Artie does best. Justifiably one of the episode's standout lines.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I didn't even need to be there for the fuckin' Saget interview

jokes.text: Yeah, love the one where the man gets hit in the nuts with the Wiffle Ball.
jokes.setup: Artie sincerely says "Love your work, Bob" to Bob Saget as he leaves
jokes.punchline: Larry's cutting addendum reduces Saget's entire body of work to America's Funniest Home Videos' lowest-common-denominator content
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry-insider comedy. Larry's contempt for Saget/AFV is delivered with just enough charm that it could be a compliment — the specific 'Wiffle Ball' detail makes it perfectly absurd. Shows the subtle cruelty beneath Larry's professional polish.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: All I said was 'Hi, Bob. Bye, Bob.' I could've been working at a Jack In The Box

jokes.text: An author, and don't panic, but Macaulay Culkin dropped out.
jokes.setup: Listing tomorrow night's guests casually
jokes.punchline: "Don't panic" followed immediately by Macaulay Culkin dropping out — the panic-stopper arrives simultaneously with panic-inducing news
jokes.explanation: Good structural comedy — the 'don't panic' is immediately undermined by panic-worthy news. Classic setup that works on the absurdity of how bad news gets delivered in a TV production context.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yeah, love the one where the man gets hit in the nuts with the Wiffle Ball

jokes.text: Donna Mills? Even Kiss is working without makeup, Artie.
jokes.setup: Network is pushing Donna Mills as a guest
jokes.punchline: Kiss working without makeup implies Donna Mills is even more dated than a legendary rock band's signature look — a sharp Hollywood-age dig
jokes.explanation: Smart showbiz dig with an unexpected cultural comparison. Using Kiss shedding their makeup as the baseline for 'things that have moved on' is both specific and original. Larry's voice — petty, cutting, pop-culture-savvy — comes through clearly.

dialogue.line: Geography quiz.
But I'm working on a new guest now.
Who's Leno got?
Macauley Culkin.
Why, you...
I'm just kidding you.

jokes.text: Larry, you know my friend Ray, host of Family Feud. We're on our way to the Smokehouse. You wanna go? We're havin' a couple beerskis.
jokes.setup: Hank introduces Larry to Ray from Family Feud in the hallway
jokes.punchline: "Beerskis" — Hank's forced, enthusiastic vernacular; the casual celebrity world of B-list TV hosts socializing together
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the milieu — Hank's social world of mid-tier TV personalities getting beers together. 'Beerskis' is a perfect Hank word: trying too hard to be a regular guy. Good character work, modest impact.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Donna Mills? Even Kiss is working without makeup, Artie

jokes.text: Beerskis. Survey says 'no.' Really.
jokes.setup: Hank invites Larry for "beerskis" with Ray from Family Feud
jokes.punchline: Larry riffs on Family Feud's catchphrase to decline — immediately followed by a sincere "Really" that deflates the wit
jokes.explanation: Elegant economy — Larry uses the Family Feud host's own show format against the invitation, then immediately adds a vulnerable 'Really' that humanizes and undercuts his own coolness. The double beat (the quip + the sincere aside) is sophisticated writing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Beerskis. Survey says 'no.' Really

jokes.text: See you Ray. Hank. [Hank responds:] Hey now.
jokes.setup: First appearance of Hank's "Hey now" catchphrase in its natural habitat
jokes.punchline: Hank deploys "hey now" as a farewell — its use as a generic greeting/farewell/filler is immediately established
jokes.explanation: The seed of the episode's central running gag. The first organic 'hey now' is perfectly timed — it plants the thing that will drive the episode's conflict. On rewatch it lands harder knowing what's coming. The phrase's meaninglessness is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey now

jokes.text: That was a fluke. The guy cares less about the show every night. Hank doesn't know a thing about the show till he's on the air. He feels it keeps him spontaneous.
jokes.setup: Post-show debrief — Artie compliments Hank's contribution
jokes.punchline: Larry's devastating multi-part critique: Hank's good moment was a fluke, he knows nothing about the show, and he's PROUD of it
jokes.explanation: Good escalating character comedy. The rhythm of complaint — fluke, cares less, knows nothing, CALLS IT SPONTANEOUS — builds into a damning portrait of Hank through Larry's eyes. Artie's defense ('it serves him well') is its own deadpan joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That was a fluke

jokes.text: Did you see him tonight practically asleep on the couch at one point? I looked... Well, who am I protecting? He was asleep on the couch.
jokes.setup: Larry starts to hedge about Hank being asleep, catches himself
jokes.punchline: "Who am I protecting?" — Larry drops his diplomatic instinct and commits to the damning truth mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: Sharp character writing. Larry's momentary instinct to protect Hank — then instantly abandoning it — reveals both his professionalism and his fundamental contempt. The self-interruption 'who am I protecting?' is the most Larry Sanders thing in the scene. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That was a fluke. The guy cares less about the show every night.

jokes.text: Of course. He's a fucking moron. What do you expect?
jokes.setup: Larry's revelation that Hank was literally asleep on air
jokes.punchline: Artie responds with total equanimity — as if Hank being a moron is a well-established fact requiring no elaboration
jokes.explanation: Classic Artie — profane, direct, utterly unsurprised. The comedy is in his total lack of outrage. 'What do you expect?' treats Hank's moronism as a natural constant, like weather. Perfect Rip Torn delivery territory.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Of course. He's a fucking moron. What do you expect?

jokes.text: All right, you guys, thank me later... Emo Phillips.
jokes.setup: Staff member announces a booking
jokes.punchline: "Emo Phillips" — the anticlimactic name drop of a deeply niche stand-up comedian as the big solution
jokes.explanation: Good industry-insider joke. The proud announcement of Emo Phillips — a cult comedian not exactly a ratings bonanza — as if it's a coup captures the desperate booking reality of late-night TV. 'Thank me later' amplifies the deluded confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What, Gallagher out of fruit?

jokes.text: What, Gallagher out of fruit?
jokes.setup: Emo Phillips announced as a guest booking
jokes.punchline: Larry dismisses it by implying Emo is only the booking when even more dated acts are unavailable — Gallagher ran out of fruit (his prop)
jokes.explanation: Excellent line. The specificity of 'Gallagher out of fruit' — referencing Gallagher's watermelon-smashing prop comedy act — as the prerequisite for booking Emo Phillips is both a perfect show-business insider joke and a devastating double-dismissal. Maximum economy, perfect character integration. One of Larry's best lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: I would've tucked him in, but there's a network TV show going on

jokes.text: I would've tucked him in, but there's a network TV show going on.
jokes.setup: Discussion about Hank falling asleep on the couch during the show
jokes.punchline: Larry frames his failure to tuck Hank in as a regrettable priority conflict — as if tending to a sleeping Hank would've been the natural instinct
jokes.explanation: Superb line. The casual absurdity of 'I would've tucked him in' paired with the completely straight 'but there's a network TV show going on' is exactly the kind of deadpan construction Larry Sanders excels at. The implicit image — Larry walking over to tuck in the sleeping Hank on live TV — is hilarious. Strong economy and character integration.

dialogue.line: Sorry. It's offensive to serial killers, isn't it?

jokes.text: You can't say 'gay.' Sorry. It's offensive to serial killers, isn't it? Which is half our audience. And the other half are victims. So we'd offend everybody with that joke.
jokes.setup: Writers reviewing a Dahmer joke and flagging the word "gay"
jokes.punchline: The reframe: the offense isn't to gay people — it's to serial killers (half the audience) and their victims (other half), so the show's entire audience would be offended
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The logic is airtight and brilliantly escalating: the word 'gay' can't be used not to protect gay people but because the REAL audience is serial killers and victims. The structure is perfect — each beat (serial killers / half / victims / other half / offend everybody) builds the absurdity methodically. Dark, subversive, and sharply written. Deserves its high score.

dialogue.line: Which is half our audience. And the other half are victims

jokes.text: We got Janet Jackson? That'd be great. Especially if she talks about the beatings she took from her father.
jokes.setup: Excited confirmation that Janet Jackson is booked
jokes.punchline: Larry's enthusiasm is conditional on Janet discussing her father's abuse — dark, specific, and completely inappropriate
jokes.explanation: Dark industry-insider joke about hosts wanting famous guests to open up about trauma — framed as Larry's real booking enthusiasm. Reveals something ugly about the talk show format itself. The specificity makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Especially if she talks about the beatings she took from her father

jokes.text: Or if she does the... I know where you're going. Got it.
jokes.setup: Larry starts to suggest another thing Janet Jackson could do on the show
jokes.punchline: Whatever Larry was gesturing toward is so obvious/inappropriate that Artie cuts him off mid-thought — the unspoken suggestion (likely referencing her appearance/sexuality) is the joke
jokes.explanation: A beautifully executed non-joke — the comedy lives entirely in what isn't said. Artie's 'I know where you're going / Got it' implies Larry's suggestion was so obviously inappropriate that verbalizing it wasn't necessary. The economy of the unspoken gag is sophisticated television writing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Maybe it looks better when it's lit. That would be my guess

jokes.text: It's a candle in the shape of your head. It's a good likeness.
jokes.setup: Beverly brings a fan letter; Larry doesn't want to see it — Artie intervenes because "some things are too good to miss"
jokes.punchline: A candle in the shape of Larry's head — unsettling fan devotion rendered in wax
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of a wax Larry-head candle works on multiple levels — creepy fan obsession, the vanity of talk show celebrity, and the deadpan 'it's a good likeness' making it weirder. Strong visual setup.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yes, or some similar piece of shit. I don't know what

jokes.text: He wrote a book about how to train your dog. It took two years to write this book. It's about dogs! To people or to dogs?
jokes.setup: Artie describes the dog expert as having spent two years writing his book
jokes.punchline: Larry: "To people or to dogs?" — questioning who the audience for a dog training book actually is
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. The rhythm of 'It's about dogs!' followed by Larry's genuine confusion about the book's readership is great deadpan construction. Larry's contempt for soft guests is perfectly captured.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: To people or to dogs?

jokes.text: Paula says his animals are like children to him, which I find very sad.
jokes.setup: Artie explains the dog expert's profound attachment to his animals
jokes.punchline: "Which I find very sad" — Artie delivers a completely sincere judgment that dismisses the guest's entire emotional life
jokes.explanation: One of Artie's best lines in the episode. The deadpan sincerity of 'which I find very sad' after a human-interest detail is perfectly Artie — world-weary, dismissive, delivered without cruelty but landing as absolutely devastating. Pure character economy.

dialogue.speaker: Producer
dialogue.line: Paula says his animals are like children to him, which I find very sad

jokes.text: Artie, do you think we need to replace Hank?
jokes.setup: Conversation about Hank's apathy and absence
jokes.punchline: The question itself — posed so casually, as if replacing the show's sidekick is a routine staffing decision
jokes.explanation: The comedic value is in the offhand delivery — Larry floats firing his longtime sidekick as if it's a minor scheduling concern. Sets up the episode's emotional stakes while being funny. The lack of response (what follows is Hank's 'hey now') makes the pause land.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey now

jokes.text: [Immediately after Larry asks about replacing Hank] Hey, Hank? — Hey now.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if they should replace Hank — then immediately calls out to him
jokes.punchline: Hank arrives/responds with "Hey now" — the thing Larry wants to suppress, deployed at the worst possible moment
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural comedy — the 'hey now' arrives in the same breath as the question of replacing Hank, creating a perfect ironic juxtaposition. The episode crystallizes its central tension in two words. Rewatch bonus: knowing the episode's trajectory makes this even sharper.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey now

jokes.text: I'd like to fuck her. You don't play for the Kings. Do you ever turn down anything?
jokes.setup: Hank watches Darlene walk away after delivering his itinerary
jokes.punchline: "You don't play for the Kings" — an absurdist non-sequitur sports metaphor for 'you're not that attractive/eligible' that makes no sense but sounds confident
jokes.explanation: Good Hank character comedy — his unsolicited sexual commentary followed by the cutting 'you don't play for the Kings' is a sharp put-down of Hank's delusions. The sports metaphor is absurd and specific enough to be funny. Classic Hank ego getting punctured.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'd like to fuck her

jokes.text: Oh, sure. [Beat] The R.V. Show at the Rose Bowl.
jokes.setup: Asked if he ever turns anything down
jokes.punchline: After a confident 'Oh, sure' — the ONE thing he turned down was the R.V. Show at the Rose Bowl, immediately undercut by it being a major national event he IS doing
jokes.explanation: Perfectly constructed Hank joke. He confidently claims to turn things down — then names the R.V. show, which turns out to be something he IS doing. His delusion that an R.V. expo is a prestigious booking that COULD be turned down captures his entire character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You don't play for the Kings. Do you ever turn down anything?

jokes.text: You know, Hank, I was just wondering why you say that 'hey now' thing. It was something you used on the show. Now you're starting to use it in your personal life. It's an affectation of some sort, isn't it? Did you ever say it as a kid?
jokes.setup: Larry pulls Hank aside privately to discuss the 'hey now'
jokes.punchline: Larry's pseudo-psychological analysis of "hey now" — treating it like a psychiatric symptom or verbal tic worthy of serious inquiry
jokes.explanation: The episode's central cringe scene begins here. Larry's earnest, analytical deconstruction of a two-word catchphrase — treating it like a significant personality disorder — is quintessential Larry Sanders awkward comedy. The 'did you ever say it as a kid?' is especially funny in its absurd therapy-speak.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, that's the biggest one in the country.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: No, that's the national one.

jokes.text: No. I probably didn't. But I said 'hey'... and I said 'now'... I mean, at different times. I never put them together till later in life. So in that sense, it's part of my personality.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Hank ever said 'hey now' as a child
jokes.punchline: Hank's earnest defense — that 'hey' and 'now' existed separately in his vocabulary before being combined — as a genuine argument for the catchphrase's authenticity
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak in pure character terms. Jeffrey Tambor's Hank constructing a sincere philosophical defense of 'hey now' — that the words existed separately before merging — is absurdist genius that could ONLY work for this specific character. It's both ridiculous and internally logical within Hank's worldview. The escalation of 'so in that sense, it's part of my personality' is devastating. Among the best Hank Kingsley moments in the series.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey now

jokes.text: Are you telling me that when you do your... [mimes Larry's flipper gesture] ...that isn't the same affectation? That isn't the same as my 'hey now'?
jokes.setup: Larry tells Hank to stop saying 'hey now'
jokes.punchline: Hank turns the tables — Larry has an affectation too (his signature pen flip/gesture), so why should Hank's be singled out?
jokes.explanation: Brilliant pivot. Hank's counter-attack — that Larry has his own affectation — is both logically sound and deeply satisfying. It reveals Larry's hypocrisy and gives Hank an unexpected moment of genuine self-defense. The visual of Hank mimicking Larry's gesture is pure character comedy gold. One of the episode's high points.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I never put them together till later in life. So in that sense, it's part of my personality

jokes.text: You just said it again, and I asked you not to say it.
jokes.setup: Hank uses 'hey now' mid-argument while arguing he should be allowed to say 'hey now'
jokes.punchline: Larry catches Hank using the forbidden phrase in the very sentence where he's defending his right to use it
jokes.explanation: Perfectly constructed comic escalation — Hank involuntarily deploys 'hey now' IN the argument about whether he should say 'hey now.' The structure is airtight and the timing is everything. Classic cringe-escalation comedy that makes the audience both laugh and cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You do this, that isn't the same affectation? That isn't the same as my 'hey now'?

jokes.text: Hey now, that was real funny.
jokes.setup: Larry challenges Hank to use 'hey now' in a sentence
jokes.punchline: Hank's example sentence is both a genuine use of 'hey now' AND an oddly pointed sarcastic comment about the argument they're having
jokes.explanation: Good double-edged construction — the example sentence functions both as a demonstration AND as a sarcastic dig at Larry, which Hank may or may not intend. The layering is elegant.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Uh, hey now, that was real funny

jokes.text: You know what, Hank? It's not even in the dictionary, 'hey now.'
jokes.setup: Hank demonstrates 'hey now' in a sentence
jokes.punchline: Larry's nuclear option: it doesn't exist as a real phrase — attempting to erase 'hey now' from language itself
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Larry's attack from 'it's annoying' to 'it doesn't literally exist in language' is a funny authoritarianism move. The pedantic dictionary argument in the context of a two-word exclamation is absurd and very Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey now!

jokes.text: You say, 'And of course, my sidekick Hank.' — 'And of course, my sidekick Hank.' — HEY NOW!
jokes.setup: Larry insists 'hey now' doesn't belong in any sentence
jokes.punchline: Hank demonstrates exactly how it functions on the show — as a Pavlovian response to his own introduction — proving it has a native context even if it's not a 'real' phrase
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic pinnacle. Hank playing BOTH Larry AND himself — doing Larry's intro in Larry's voice, then snapping into 'HEY NOW!' — is a moment of pure genius. It reveals that 'hey now' has a completely valid context, making Larry's objection suddenly petty, and it's also an absolutely perfect encapsulation of Hank's entire role on the show. Exceptional character integration, structure, and economy. This is what the episode has been building to.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: By interplay, you mean the times we're both awake?

jokes.text: I think it helps make the show work. It's part of our whole interplay on camera. By interplay, you mean the times we're both awake?
jokes.setup: Hank defends 'hey now' as part of their on-air chemistry
jokes.punchline: Larry's response redefines "interplay" as "the rare moments when Hank isn't asleep" — a perfect callback to the sleeping-on-couch revelation
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback construction. Taking Hank's earnest defense of 'interplay' and redefining it through the lens of his earlier sleeping incident is devastating and funny. The economy is perfect — 'the times we're both awake' does enormous damage in very few words. Among the episode's top lines.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Now, LaToya, she could circle. There's a gal that could be circling for years

jokes.text: She's not coming, is she? She's not coming. You said she's landing. She could be circling. She's going to land.
jokes.setup: Producer assures Larry that Janet Jackson is coming — 'she's landing as we speak'
jokes.punchline: Larry's deadpan skepticism ('she's not coming') vs. the producer's increasingly desperate insistence ('she could be circling') — the euphemisms for 'she cancelled' getting more absurd
jokes.explanation: Good TV production cringe — the producer trapped between lying and admitting failure, using aviation language to defer bad news. Larry's clairvoyant certainty ('she's not coming') versus the producer's desperate 'circling' is funny industry-insider reality.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: When I met him, he was just a cruise director.

jokes.text: Now, LaToya, she could circle. There's a gal that could be circling for years. Feel free to put that in your monologue.
jokes.setup: Larry says Janet Jackson could be circling the airport
jokes.punchline: Artie extends the metaphor to LaToya Jackson — the less famous Jackson sibling who could orbit indefinitely without anyone noticing
jokes.explanation: Sharp celebrity-roast style dig delivered with Artie's characteristic economy. 'There's a gal that could be circling for years' uses the circling metaphor to devastating effect on LaToya's relevance. The addition of 'feel free to put that in your monologue' shows Artie's awareness that he's funnier than Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Jeannie
dialogue.line: After the show, talk to him. It's not as if you have a million friends

jokes.text: It's not as if you have a million friends.
jokes.setup: Suggesting Larry should forgive Hank and talk to him
jokes.punchline: The reminder that Larry's social circle is thin — framed as a reason to preserve the Hank friendship
jokes.explanation: Sharp, cutting, true — this is one of those Larry Sanders observations that lands because it's probably accurate. The show's underlying loneliness under the Hollywood gloss is suddenly visible. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I would settle for Tito at this point. I just want you to know that

jokes.text: I'm your friend.
jokes.setup: Someone notes that Larry doesn't have many friends
jokes.punchline: Artie's sincere-but-flat declaration — coming from a gruff man who doesn't do warmth — lands as both genuinely touching and somehow funny
jokes.explanation: Two words, delivered flat, from Rip Torn's Artie — the comedy lives entirely in the character and performance context. It's simultaneously the realest and funniest thing said in this scene. Maximum economy, maximum character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I've seen terrorists do it

jokes.text: And now, 'fresh from her Rhythm Nation tour, please welcome...' Dear God, if there's any justice in this world... 'Janet Jackson.' Don't write that part.
jokes.setup: Artie drafts the Janet Jackson introduction
jokes.punchline: Mid-intro, Artie inserts his private prayer "Dear God, if there's any justice in this world" — breaking the copy with genuine desperation — then remembers to clarify "Don't write that part"
jokes.explanation: Exceptional comedy construction. Artie's prayer inserted mid-dictation of an intro copy — treating 'Dear God, if there's any justice' as a functional sentence in a professional broadcast document — is both absurd and perfectly in character. The 'Don't write that part' kicker is the ideal button. One of the episode's strongest moments.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I thought I just heard you say, 'my half.' Is that what you just said? My half of the show, Hank?

jokes.text: I would settle for Tito at this point. I just want you to know that.
jokes.setup: They've already lost Janet Jackson; the situation is deteriorating
jokes.punchline: Tito Jackson — the most invisible Jackson — as the bar Artie has now lowered himself to
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the Jackson sibling hierarchy gag — from Janet to LaToya to now Tito, each one a lower rung. 'I just want you to know that' sells Artie's resigned sincerity. The Jackson ranking comedy chain across three jokes is a strong running bit.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You look a little like Kitty in Gunsmoke

jokes.text: And don't do that. I know you think it calms me. I've seen terrorists do it.
jokes.setup: Someone (producer/Sid) makes a calming gesture toward Larry
jokes.punchline: "I've seen terrorists do it" — Larry's paranoid mind connects a calming gesture to terrorist behavior
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Larry paranoia line. The leap from 'that calming hand gesture' to 'terrorists also do that' is pure Larry Sanders — anxious, conspiratorial, and absolutely convinced of his own logic. The specificity of 'terrorists' over any gentler alternative makes it perfectly absurd. High quotability, very Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Why don't you shove it up your ass? Or do you already do that commercial?

jokes.text: Listen, I want you to know it's not the 'hey now' thing I'm mad about and it's not that you fall asleep on the couch.
jokes.setup: Larry calls Hank in for what seems like a reconciliation
jokes.punchline: Larry opens with the two EXACT things he's clearly mad about, framed as 'not the issue' — classic passive-aggressive non-apology construction
jokes.explanation: Effective character comedy — Larry's passive-aggressive opener names the exact issues as non-issues, which is more revealing than any direct accusation. Classic conflict-avoidant character behavior played for comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Makeup person
dialogue.line: Fine, if you want your face and hands to clash.

jokes.text: I don't fall asleep! I pay attention. I am there.
jokes.setup: Larry brings up the sleeping-on-couch issue (while claiming it's not the issue)
jokes.punchline: Hank's emphatic triple denial — 'I don't fall asleep! I pay attention. I am there.' — each phrase more desperately unconvincing than the last
jokes.explanation: Good character moment. The escalating denial culminating in the weirdly existential 'I am there' — a statement about physical presence rather than awareness — is funny for how obviously false it is. Classic Hank denial.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey now!

jokes.text: I thought I just heard you say 'my half.' Is that what you just said? My half of the show, Hank?
jokes.setup: Larry tells Hank to worry about 'your half' of the show
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately seizes on Hank's casual use of 'my half' as an ownership claim — the paranoid read of a harmless phrase
jokes.explanation: Excellent Larry Sanders paranoia comedy. The way Larry processes 'your half' as a territorial claim is a perfect distillation of his insecurity — the host who sees ownership threats everywhere. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Janet Jackson is out, T. Bone Burnett is in. You were right. She was circling. She got diverted to Reno.

jokes.text: What the hell is that? This is a corset. Why you wearing it? Because I believe it makes me look thinner, and it does.
jokes.setup: In the middle of their argument, Larry notices something under Hank's shirt
jokes.punchline: Hank is wearing a corset — and defends it with total sincerity and misplaced confidence ('and it does')
jokes.explanation: Perfect visual comedy that works beautifully as character comedy too. The corset is deeply Hank — vain, insecure about appearance, wearing garments from another era. His absolute certainty that 'it does' make him look thinner is beautiful. The discovery mid-argument is wonderful comedic timing.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: and me... hey now... Hank Kingsley

jokes.text: You look a little like Kitty in Gunsmoke.
jokes.setup: Hank is wearing a corset and believes it makes him look thinner
jokes.punchline: Larry compares the corset-wearing Hank to Kitty from Gunsmoke — a saloon madam in a 19th-century Western
jokes.explanation: Exceptional comedy — the specificity of 'Kitty in Gunsmoke' as the reference for a corset-wearing man is both wildly unexpected and perfectly precise. It's the funniest possible comparison: not just 'a woman' but specifically a TV Western saloon keeper. The cultural specificity and the image of Tambor in that role is inspired. High originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: What do you mean, there's no helicopters? For God's sakes, tell 'em he's a burn victim.

jokes.text: Why don't you shove it up your ass? Or do you already do that commercial?
jokes.setup: Larry insults Hank's corset appearance
jokes.punchline: Hank fires back with a standard insult — then Larry immediately deflects it by suggesting it might be a commercial opportunity
jokes.explanation: Sharp two-beat exchange. Hank's insult is conventional but Larry's pivot — turning the anatomical suggestion into a product endorsement inquiry — is a perfect Larry move. It simultaneously deflects the anger and reminds us of Hank's commercial-whoring.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If he were a kidney, he'd been here an hour ago

jokes.text: No, I don't. That's a good idea. Thanks. I'll call my agent. I'd like some of the commission, by the way.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Hank already does a commercial for shoving things up his ass
jokes.punchline: Hank briefly objects, then genuinely considers it as a business opportunity — Larry demands commission for the idea
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the commercial joke — Hank momentarily takes the absurd pitch seriously before course-correcting, and Larry's demand for commission is a perfect cap that reflects both their mercenary showbiz relationship and the underlying tension.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If I had a gun, I'd put it in my mouth, turn and take us both out

jokes.text: I don't need any hand makeup. Fine, if you want your face and hands to clash.
jokes.setup: Larry resists hand makeup from the makeup artist
jokes.punchline: Makeup artist's dry correction: refusing hand makeup means face and hands will visibly clash — delivered as a professional judgment
jokes.explanation: Good dry industry joke — the absurd specificity of matching face and hand makeup tones as a real professional concern captures the vanity of broadcast TV perfectly. The makeup artist's tone is perfectly flat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He's written a wonderful book called My Dog, Myself. Teaching us how to train a dog in five days... and we are up to approximately day four.

jokes.text: When I say 'three,' can you give me a 'hey now'? Ready? One, two, three. Hey now! Very, very good.
jokes.setup: Hank addresses the studio audience before the show
jokes.punchline: Hank trains the audience to say 'hey now' — the catchphrase Larry hates becomes a rehearsed crowd response, deepening its permanence
jokes.explanation: Perfect dramatic irony — Hank, freshly told by Larry to suppress 'hey now,' immediately teaches the AUDIENCE to say it, ensuring its immortality. The power reversal is elegant and very funny. Knowing Larry's objection makes this significantly funnier. Strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank has had a dog. Okay. Well, I thought you might've, in fact, had a dog

jokes.text: Janet Jackson is out, T. Bone Burnett is in. You were right. She was circling. She got diverted to Reno. Fucking fog.
jokes.setup: Janet Jackson was supposed to be the big get; Larry predicted she wasn't coming
jokes.punchline: She was literally circling (as per Artie's joke), got diverted to Reno — the replacement is T. Bone Burnett, and the excuse is fog
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the circling joke is satisfying — she WAS circling, it's confirmed. The matter-of-fact 'Fucking fog' as the explanation for losing a major celebrity guest is a perfect show-business shrug. Larry's expletive-free 'you were right' acknowledgment is understated.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Philipe Xavier Kingsley

jokes.text: Tonight join Larry and his guests Earl Holliman, T. Bone Burnett, dog expert Carl Henkel, and me... hey now... Hank Kingsley.
jokes.setup: The on-air show opens with Hank doing the intro announcements
jokes.punchline: Hank inserts 'hey now' into his own on-air introduction — the catchphrase now embedded in the official broadcast
jokes.explanation: The running gag reaches its inevitable peak: 'hey now' is now canonized in the official broadcast opening. The comma-pause before 'hey now' mid-sentence makes it feel both accidental and deliberate. Larry's had his say; the phrase has won. Excellent structural payoff on the episode's central comic thread.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He can never stop... licking himself.

jokes.text: You said he'd be here ten minutes ago. What if we copter him in? What do you mean, there's no helicopters? For God's sakes, tell 'em he's a burn victim. If he were a kidney, he'd been here an hour ago.
jokes.setup: T. Bone Burnett is late; Artie is managing the crisis backstage
jokes.punchline: "Tell 'em he's a burn victim" / "If he were a kidney, he'd been here an hour ago" — Artie's problem-solving involves medical fraud and organ transplant envy
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's absolute best jokes. The escalation is perfect: helicopter → no helicopters → fake burn victim → kidney comparison. Each beat is more insane than the last. 'If he were a kidney, he'd been here an hour ago' is a genuine comic masterpiece — unexpected, perfectly logical within its own absurdity, and entirely Artie. This is the caliber of the 8.0 anchor joke or above. Highly quotable, rewatch essential.

dialogue.line: I believe that's learned behavior. When you stop, the dog will stop

jokes.text: If I had a gun, I'd put it in my mouth, turn and take us both out.
jokes.setup: Artie tells Larry that Earl Holliman sings, suggesting a segment filler
jokes.punchline: Larry's response to the prospect of Earl Holliman singing is suicidal ideation — extended to homicide
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark comedy — Larry's suicidal-then-homicidal despair at the prospect of a lounge-singer-segment is perfectly calibrated. 'Turn and take us both out' is a great escalation of the standard mouth-gun image. Strong character integration: only Larry Sanders would express professional despair this specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I think that is... It's that old 'monkey see, monkey do.'

jokes.text: I can't wait to read that book.
jokes.setup: In the middle of backstage chaos about missing guests and singing Earl Holliman
jokes.punchline: Larry deadpans about eagerness to read the dog expert's book — total non-sequitur sincerity in the midst of professional crisis
jokes.explanation: Dry, minimal laugh — Larry's non sequitur enthusiasm about the dog book in the middle of a crisis is a good deadpan beat. Works better in context than on paper.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I would just cut out the middleman there and lick him

jokes.text: I found your book, if I may say, fascinating... and have enjoyed thoroughly talking to you about dogs... and myself.
jokes.setup: On-air Larry introduces the dog expert's book 'My Dog, Myself'
jokes.punchline: The on-air Larry, reading the title 'My Dog, Myself,' pauses and then adds 'and myself' — converting a talk-show pleasantry into unintended narcissism via the book's title
jokes.explanation: Brilliant construction — Larry's standard effusive host praise ('I found your book fascinating... talking to you about dogs') suddenly veers into narcissism with 'and myself' because the BOOK TITLE demands it. It reveals Larry's genuine self-absorption while being technically accurate. Elegant joke that only works with this specific book title.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, boy. I couldn't... I would just cut out the middleman there and lick him.

jokes.text: My dog Philipe... Philipe Xavier Kingsley.
jokes.setup: Hank gets the opportunity to engage with the dog expert on air
jokes.punchline: Hank's dog has a full formal name — Philipe Xavier Kingsley — delivered as if this is completely normal
jokes.explanation: Perfect Hank character comedy — giving his dog a francophilic full name including his own last name (Kingsley) is delightfully Hank: vain, social-climbing, treating the dog as a status symbol. Larry's 'I did not recall that' is a great straight-man response.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: "Sometimes" is the key phrase

jokes.text: My dog has a particular problem. He can never stop... licking himself.
jokes.setup: Hank asks the dog expert for help with his dog's problem — building a long pause
jokes.punchline: The dog licks himself — a delayed, slightly deflated punchline after the elaborate setup suggesting something worse
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the bigger jokes to follow. The misdirection is relatively obvious — it's clearly going somewhere sexual — but serves as a necessary foundation for the escalating dog-licking comedy sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah. Cutting into Hank's action, in effect

jokes.text: I believe that's learned behavior. When you stop, the dog will stop.
jokes.setup: Hank's dog compulsively licks himself
jokes.punchline: Carl's professional diagnosis implies Hank also licks himself — the 'learned behavior' from owner to dog
jokes.explanation: Sharp and economical — the dog expert's completely straight professional advice implicating Hank as the source of the behavior is a perfect build. 'When you stop, the dog will stop' achieves maximum implication with no vulgarity. The deadpan delivery is everything.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And I'm thinking, maybe I ought to get a dog costume

jokes.text: Well, something has to give, because he used to lick himself and then kiss me on the face.
jokes.setup: The dog licking sequence continues
jokes.punchline: Hank's complaint reveals the full disgusting chain: dog licks himself → kisses Hank → on the face
jokes.explanation: Good escalation in the dog-licking sequence. The specificity of 'on the face' versus anywhere else makes it appropriately disgusting and funny. The straight-faced delivery by Hank makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Carl
dialogue.line: If you call our office at Actors and Others for Animals... we can get you neutered for a very low cost

jokes.text: I couldn't... I would just cut out the middleman there and lick him. By the way, none of this is covered in my book.
jokes.setup: Hank describes the dog licking himself then kissing him
jokes.punchline: Larry suggests Hank should just lick the dog directly — 'cut out the middleman' — then the dog expert deadpans that this isn't in his book
jokes.explanation: Larry's 'cut out the middleman' suggestion is the right kind of on-air host provocateur comedy, and the dog expert's hapless 'none of this is covered in my book' is a perfect straight-man button that validates the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: We do not have the cover... but this is what it looks like once you open it. This is what you play. Really, what good does the cover do you?

jokes.text: But sometimes I would have a lady come back to the house... 'Sometimes' is the key phrase.
jokes.setup: Hank continues his dog problem story and mentions bringing women home
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate aside: 'Sometimes is the key phrase' — a dig at Hank's sexual frequency that Hank either doesn't hear or ignores
jokes.explanation: A perfect quick-draw Larry zinger — he seizes on 'sometimes' as the revealing word in Hank's story, exposing the vanity of his sidekick. Delivered as an aside while Hank continues, it's exactly how Larry's cruelty operates: under the radar but devastating. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Really, what good does the cover do you? His new album is called The Criminal Under My Own Hat

jokes.text: Philipe would put his nose in a... How do you say this on television? In an awkward place.
jokes.setup: Hank describes his dog's embarrassing behavior with female guests
jokes.punchline: "In an awkward place" — the TV-appropriate euphemism for the dog nosing a woman's groin
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — the TV-appropriate self-censorship is a slight meta moment. Hank's pausing to consider broadcast standards while telling a story that shouldn't be on television is amusing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You saved my ass.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And I did it without saying 'hey now.'

jokes.text: He hadn't even met her.
jokes.setup: Hank's dog nosing women in awkward places
jokes.punchline: Hank's complaint is not the behavior itself but the lack of social protocol — the dog violated introductory etiquette
jokes.explanation: The funniest single line in the episode. 'He hadn't even met her' reframes the dog's groin-nosing as a social etiquette violation — as if the behavior would be perfectly acceptable post-introduction. The logic is both absurd and somehow coherent. Perfect economy (four words), maximum impact. This is the episode's funniest moment and would be quotable in any comedy context.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And I did it without saying 'hey now.'

jokes.text: Yeah. Cutting into Hank's action, in effect.
jokes.setup: Dog nosing women in awkward places at Hank's apartment
jokes.punchline: Larry frames it as the dog competing with Hank for sexual territory — implying Hank and his dog operate at the same level
jokes.explanation: Good quick follow — Larry immediately finds the sexual competition angle and lands it with good economy. The phrase 'Hank's action' implies Hank's own moves aren't much more sophisticated than the dog's.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You could go with me on those other jobs. They would love to have you there.

jokes.text: The woman always says, 'That's okay. He doesn't know what he's doing.' And I'm thinking, maybe I ought to get a dog costume.
jokes.setup: Women excuse the dog's inappropriate behavior
jokes.punchline: Hank considers dressing as a dog to receive the same social pardon for equivalent behavior
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation and payoff. Hank's conclusion — that a dog costume would grant him the same social immunity as the dog — is perfectly logical within the absurdity and reveals something genuinely dark about Hank's desires. The delivery is key: it's sincere, not jokey. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That's okay. I've turned into a moron

jokes.text: If you call our office at Actors and Others for Animals, we can get you neutered for a very low cost.
jokes.setup: Hank considers dressing as a dog to get away with inappropriate behavior
jokes.punchline: The dog expert suggests neutering Hank — routing the human through the animal behavior correction system
jokes.explanation: Great button from the dog expert — the most logical answer to a man considering dog behavior as a sexual strategy. 'For a very low cost' is the perfect deadpan add, making it feel like a genuine charitable service. The expert maintaining his professional demeanor throughout makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I've turned into an asshole last couple of years.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That's okay. I've turned into a moron.

jokes.text: Why is T. Bone chasing Paula?
jokes.setup: T. Bone Burnett has finally arrived backstage
jokes.punchline: His arrival is announced not by a handshake but by apparently chasing the producer through the building — introduced mid-chaos
jokes.explanation: Good visual comedy inferred from dialogue — T. Bone Burnett, the late-arriving musician, is introduced by chasing a producer. The image is unexpected and funny. The line's economy is excellent — 'Why is T. Bone chasing Paula?' does all the work.

jokes.text: We do not have the cover... but this is what it looks like once you open it. This is what you play. Really, what good does the cover do you?
jokes.setup: Larry introduces T. Bone Burnett's album 'The Criminal Under My Own Hat'
jokes.punchline: They don't have the album cover — only the open record — and Larry rationalizes this is actually the useful part anyway
jokes.explanation: Excellent production-mishap comedy. Larry's recovery logic — 'what good does the cover do you?' — is both a genuine rationalization and a meta-joke about album promotion. The image of a talk show host holding only the inner sleeve of a record is funny. Larry's composure under production chaos is a character highlight.

jokes.text: You saved my ass. That's my job. And I did it without saying 'hey now.'
jokes.setup: T. Bone's performance saves the show; Larry thanks Hank backstage
jokes.punchline: Hank's pointed observation that he saved the show WITHOUT saying 'hey now' — implying Larry's earlier criticism was wrong, and that Hank is more capable than given credit for
jokes.explanation: Beautiful structural irony — the episode's payoff on the 'hey now' conflict. Hank uses his not-saying-'hey now' as a competitive point against Larry, which both closes the arc and reveals Hank's wounded pride underneath. It's a funny line that carries genuine emotional weight. Strong character integration and callback.

jokes.text: I'm sorry about that. I was upset that you do those other jobs. You could go with me on those other jobs. They would love to have you there.
jokes.setup: Hank apologizes and invites Larry to his side gigs
jokes.punchline: The R.V. Show and shopping mall openings as a genuine invitation for Larry to join — Hank's world is these commercial appearances
jokes.explanation: Good character irony — Hank's sincere invitation reveals his total lack of self-awareness about the hierarchy between his gigs and Larry's show. 'They would love to have you there' about an R.V. expo is both touching and funny.

jokes.text: Look, I fell asleep on the couch. I'm sorry. Don't lecture me anymore. I can't help it. I've turned into an asshole last couple of years.
jokes.setup: Reconciliation between Larry and Hank
jokes.punchline: Larry admits he's become an asshole — delivered with more resignation than remorse, as if it's simply a career development
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy with emotional resonance. 'I've turned into an asshole last couple of years' — delivered without drama, as if describing a professional evolution — is very Larry. The self-awareness without self-correction is funny and true to the character.

jokes.text: That's okay. I've turned into a moron.
jokes.setup: Larry admits he's become an asshole
jokes.punchline: Hank's symmetrical counter-admission — he's turned into a moron — delivered as if these are equivalent career paths that make their partnership work
jokes.explanation: The episode's finest moment and among the best lines in the series. The symmetry is mathematically perfect: Larry admits to being an asshole; Hank admits to being a moron. The deadpan parallel structure — 'That's okay. I've turned into a moron' — has the formal elegance of a great sitcom button while being the most emotionally honest thing either character says all episode. It's funny, it's true, it explains their entire relationship, and it leaves you smiling AND slightly sad. This is the caliber that warrants the highest scores in the episode.

jokes.text: I mean, have a good time with it.
jokes.setup: Hank admits he's turned into a moron
jokes.punchline: Larry's response to learning his sidekick has become a moron: 'Have a good time with it' — absurdly casual life advice about embracing one's own intellectual decline
jokes.explanation: A perfect kicker to the episode's emotional climax. 'Have a good time with it' is both warm and devastating — it accepts Hank's moronism as a terminal condition and offers the best available advice. The tone is somewhere between genuine friendship and absurdist resignation. Excellent final beat.

tmdb_overview: Hank falls asleep during the show, which is just the last straw for a fed-up Larry.
